paragraph: At the start of the story, Dickens shows that Scrooge likes to keep people [[away]]. He describes him as “secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster”. An oyster has a hard [[shell]] that closes around its soft body. Scrooge does something [[similar]] when he shuts other people out. Keeping to himself may help him feel [[safe]], but it also makes it hard for anyone to get close. Dickens gives the reader a reason to wonder what Scrooge might be [[protecting]].

Dickens shows how [[difficult]] it is to get through to Scrooge by describing him as “Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever [[struck]] out generous fire”. A hard stone does not bend easily, and a sharp [[edge]] can cut you. In the same way, Scrooge is hard to persuade and can hurt people with his [[replies]]. The words “generous fire” give us an idea of the warmth we might hope to [[find]] in him. So far, nobody has managed to bring it out.

Scrooge dismisses Christmas as soon as Fred wishes him a [[merry]] one. He answers with “Bah!” and then “Humbug!” The first word sounds like a [[noise]] he makes because he is fed up. The second suggests that he thinks there is something false about the whole celebration - “humbug” used to [[mean]] something that was a trick. Dickens shows that Scrooge has no patience for Christmas. He feels it’s just an excuse to [[pretend]] to be nice. A modern Christmas almost seems the same way - it’s supposed to be about goodwill, but it’s [[actually]] just about presents. So maybe Scrooge has a point here!

Scrooge uses money as a reason to [[refuse]] help. He explains that he does not celebrate Christmas himself and says, “I can’t [[afford]] to make idle people merry.” The words “can’t afford” make it sound as if he hasn’t got any money to [[give]]. The word “idle” tells us that he assumes the people who need help are too lazy to work. This [[opinion]] is reflected by a lot of people today who think that the poor are poor because they’re lazy, though the [[truth]] is often far from that.

When the gentlemen ask Scrooge to give money to the poor, he [[answers]] by asking, “Are there no prisons?” He then asks, “And the Union workhouses?” Scrooge already knows that these places [[exist]] - and that his taxes pay for them! His questions suggest that he thinks the poor have [[somewhere]] to go and that he has done enough. But a reader can notice how quickly he moves from hearing that people [[need]] help to making them someone else’s problem. Scrooge also doesn’t acknowledge that conditions in those places were terrible - or that [[poverty]] is not a crime to be punished with prison!

Dickens shows how cruel Scrooge can be when he [[talks]] about people he has never met. When Scrooge hears that some people would rather die than go to a [[workhouse]], he says that “they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population”. The word “surplus” [[means]] that there is too much of something. By using it about people, Scrooge makes their deaths sound like an easy way to solve a [[problem]]. But killing people is not a solution, though the way that poverty was treated back then meant that [[death]] was often the result of poverty.

Marley explains that he helped to create his own [[punishment]]. He tells Scrooge, “I wear the chain I forged in life”. To [[forge]] a chain, someone has to shape the metal and make each link. It takes time and work. Dickens [[uses]] that idea to show how Marley’s choices built up over many years until they became a chain he had to [[carry]]. When the reader sees what those choices have cost Marley, it becomes [[easier]] to imagine where Scrooge’s own choices might lead.

Marley wants Scrooge to think again about what it [[means]] to be good at business. When Scrooge praises him as a [[businessman]], Marley replies, “Mankind was my business.” Scrooge is thinking about the work they did to earn money. Marley [[uses]] the same word, “business”, to talk about his duty to other people. He has [[understood]] this too late. Dickens is arguing that people, society, and the human condition should be our “business” and not just things that are [[connected]] to making money.

Fred thinks Christmas can help people feel [[closer]] to one another. He says that people can see each other as “fellow-passengers to the grave”. [[Imagine]] sitting next to someone on a long journey. You may have very [[different]] lives, but for a while you are travelling together. Fred uses that picture to remind Scrooge that [[rich]] and poor people share the same end. Dickens gives Fred a simple way to [[explain]] why someone else’s troubles should matter to us.

Dickens shows that Scrooge’s loneliness began when he was [[young]]. The Ghost of Christmas Past tells him, “A solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still.” The word “solitary” [[reminds]] us of the oyster at the start of the book. This [[time]], though, we see a child who has been left behind while others have gone home. The word “neglected” suggests that people who could have cared for him [[failed]] to do so. Dickens gives the reader a reason to feel [[sorry]] for the boy before thinking again about the man he becomes.

Watching Fezziwig helps Scrooge see how much [[power]] a boss has over the people who work for him. Scrooge says, “The happiness he gives, is quite as great as if it cost a [[fortune]].” The word “gives” matters because Fezziwig can make people happy by the way he speaks to them and [[treats]] them. Scrooge knows how that feels because he once worked for him. Dickens [[lets]] us hear Scrooge praise the kind of boss he could choose to be for Bob Cratchit. It also shows that happiness doesn’t have a [[value]] in gold.

Belle sees that Scrooge has given money the most [[important]] place in his life. She tells him, “Another idol has displaced me”, and [[explains]] that it is “A golden one.” An idol is something people worship. By calling gold an idol, Belle [[suggests]] that Scrooge now gives it the love and attention he once gave her. Dickens lets us hear what this [[change]] looks like to someone who loves him. Scrooge may feel safer with more money, but the reader can see what he is [[losing]] as he gains it.

Dickens makes two problems easy to see by giving them the [[faces]] of children. The Ghost of Christmas Present tells Scrooge, “This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want.” Here, “Want” [[means]] having too little of what you need, such as food or warm [[clothes]]. “Ignorance” means knowing too little about what is happening to other people. Scrooge can turn away from a conversation about [[poverty]] quite easily. When Dickens puts two children right in front of him, it becomes much [[harder]] for him, or for the reader, to look away.

The Ghost of Christmas Present makes Scrooge hear how [[harsh]] his own words sounded. When Scrooge asks if anyone can help the two children, the Ghost [[replies]], “Are there no prisons?” and then, “Are there no workhouses?” These are questions Scrooge used when he wanted the gentlemen to leave him [[alone]]. Now that he can see the children, those answers seem far less acceptable. Dickens shows that it is easy to ignore [[suffering]] when it is just something you hear about, but when you are faced with it, in the form of a [[starving]] child, it is far harder to turn your face away.

Scrooge begins to understand the [[harm]] in his words when he learns that Tiny Tim may die. The Ghost repeats Scrooge’s [[remark]] about the “surplus population”, and Dickens says that Scrooge is “overcome with penitence and grief”. “Penitence” means feeling sorry for something you have [[done]]. “Grief” tells us how deeply sad he feels. Scrooge is upset about what might happen to Tim, and he feels [[ashamed]] of what he said earlier. By bringing his old words back at this moment, Dickens [[lets]] the reader see a change in how Scrooge feels.

Dickens makes Scrooge face where his way of life might [[lead]]. The Ghost points to a grave, and Scrooge reads “upon the stone of the [[neglected]] grave his own name, Ebenezer Scrooge”. We have heard the word “neglected” before, when the Ghost of Christmas Past showed Scrooge as a [[child]] left on his own. As a boy, he had little choice about being alone. As a man, he often [[chooses]] to keep people away. By bringing the same word back at the grave, Dickens shows how the loneliness of Scrooge’s [[childhood]] might follow him to the end of his life.

Scrooge promises to treat people differently for the rest of his [[life]]. He tells the Ghost, “I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year.” The words “in my heart” [[suggest]] that Christmas now means something to him personally. By saying “all the year”, he promises to carry its [[kindness]] into ordinary days as well. The word “try” makes his promise sound like something he knows will take [[effort]]. Dickens ends the book by telling us that Scrooge did all he said he would, so we [[know]] he did it, even though it was hard.

When Scrooge wakes up on Christmas morning, he can [[hardly]] find enough words for how happy he feels. He cries, “I am as light as a [[feather]], I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a schoolboy.” The feather makes his joy sound like a [[weight]] has been lifted - perhaps the weight of guilt at being so miserly. The schoolboy makes us think of the child he [[once]] was and reminds us that he has re-learnt his innocence. Dickens keeps the comparisons coming so quickly that the reader can [[hear]] Scrooge getting carried away with his own excitement.

Scrooge shows that his change will make a real [[difference]] to Bob Cratchit. Bob arrives late and expects his boss to tell him off. Instead, Scrooge [[announces]], “I am about to raise your salary!” Earlier, he complained about [[paying]] Bob for a day off. Now he chooses to pay him more. Dickens lets us share Bob’s [[surprise]], but the pay rise also means something after the joke is over. Bob will [[have]] more money to take home to his family.

By the end of the story, Scrooge takes a [[lasting]] interest in someone else’s life. Dickens tells us that “to Tiny Tim, who did not die, he was a second [[father]]”. Calling him a “second father” suggests that Scrooge keeps looking after Tim over time. It also shows how [[close]] they have become. The man who once wanted to be left alone now has a place in a [[family]] that needs him. Dickens lets the reader see what Scrooge [[gains]] by making room in his life for someone else.

Dickens ends the story by sharing Tiny Tim’s [[blessing]] with the reader. The narrator closes with the words “And so, as Tiny Tim observed, God [[bless]] Us, Every One!” The words “Every One” are easy to read past, but think about who they [[include]]. They include the Cratchits, Fred, the reader, and even Scrooge. Earlier, Scrooge talked as though some people could be counted as [[surplus]]. By giving the last words to a blessing that leaves nobody out, Dickens asks us to think about who we might have been [[leaving]] out ourselves.

Dickens presents Scrooge’s isolation as something he actively [[maintains]]. The narrator describes him as “secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster”. The repeated “and” [[adds]] one sign of separation after another, until the oyster gives those qualities a physical shape. Its [[shell]] protects what is inside, but it also forms a [[barrier]]. When the Ghost of Christmas Past shows Scrooge as a lonely child, the reader can begin to see why keeping others at a [[distance]] might once have felt safer to him.

Dickens’s image of flint makes Scrooge seem both difficult to [[influence]] and capable of hurting others. He is described as “Hard and sharp as flint, from which no [[steel]] had ever struck out generous fire”. While “hard” suggests that appeals for help make little [[impression]] on him, “sharp” suggests that his replies can wound the people who approach him. Yet the word “ever” [[describes]] what has happened up to this point. The reader can wonder whether the visits from the spirits will [[finally]] bring out the warmth the narrator has found missing.

Dickens uses Scrooge’s brief reply to show how [[readily]] he dismisses Fred’s good wishes. “Bah!” makes his irritation audible, while “Humbug!” suggests that he [[regards]] Christmas as a kind of pretence. There is hardly any room for discussion in two [[exclamations]]. Fred, by comparison, takes time to explain why Christmas matters to him. The [[difference]] in their speech lets the reader hear how quickly Scrooge shuts down an [[invitation]] to share in something he has already decided is worthless.

Scrooge presents his refusal to give as a [[matter]] of what he can afford. He tells the gentlemen that he does not make [[merry]] himself and “can’t afford to make idle people merry”. The adjective “idle” turns a lack of money into a [[fault]] in the people asking for help. Dickens exposes the limits of this reasoning later, when Scrooge remembers how much [[happiness]] Fezziwig could give through a word or a look. The reader is invited to [[question]] what Scrooge really thinks he would lose by being generous.

Dickens shows how Scrooge uses public [[institutions]] to put responsibility for the poor at a distance. He asks, “Are there no prisons?” and [[follows]] this with “And the Union workhouses?” The questions sound as though the [[existence]] of these places should settle the matter. Putting prisons and workhouses together also makes poverty sound like something to [[punish]]. When the Ghost of Christmas Present turns similar questions back on Scrooge, Dickens makes him face the people his [[original]] answer allowed him to dismiss.

Scrooge’s phrase “decrease the surplus population” makes the [[deaths]] of poor people sound like a sensible adjustment. The verb “decrease” is usually [[used]] to talk about numbers, while “surplus” suggests that some people are an excess society can do without. Dickens lets that [[language]] sound cold before the reader knows Tiny Tim. Once the Ghost uses the same words about a [[child]] Scrooge wants to save, it becomes much harder for Scrooge to talk about [[poverty]] as though it were simply a problem of numbers.

Marley’s chain gives a visible form to the [[consequences]] of his choices. When he tells Scrooge, “I wear the chain I forged in life”, the verb “forged” [[suggests]] work done over time. Each link can be understood as another choice Marley made, until the [[whole]] chain became a burden he could no longer escape. Dickens makes this a warning for Scrooge, whose [[habits]] are already much like Marley’s. The reader can see why a single generous act would be only the [[beginning]] of a change in how he lives.

When Marley declares that “Mankind was my business”, he [[takes]] a word that Scrooge understands and gives it a much wider meaning. Scrooge has just [[praised]] Marley for being good at business, so the repeated word forces him to reconsider what a [[successful]] life looks like. “Mankind” extends Marley’s duty far beyond the people who paid him. Dickens later shows Scrooge [[acting]] on that lesson when he raises Bob’s salary. The reader sees how a [[businessman]] can use his position to improve another person’s life.

Fred’s image of people as “fellow-passengers to the grave” [[challenges]] Scrooge’s habit of sorting people by wealth. Calling them “fellow-passengers” suggests that they share a [[journey]] even if they have very different lives. The word “grave” gives that cheerful Christmas speech a [[serious]] edge, which becomes clearer when Scrooge sees his own grave. By [[placing]] Fred’s speech early in the story, Dickens gives the reader an idea to carry into that later scene. Scrooge must decide how to [[spend]] the time he shares with other people.

Dickens changes the reader’s view of Scrooge by [[returning]] to the word “solitary”. The Ghost of Christmas Past shows him “A solitary child, [[neglected]] by his friends”, who “is left there still”. At the start of the book, being solitary seems to [[suit]] the adult Scrooge. Here, “neglected” and “left” show that the boy’s loneliness comes from what other people have [[done]]. The echo helps the reader understand how keeping his distance as an adult may have grown out of an [[experience]] he had little power to change.

Fezziwig’s party helps Scrooge recognise that an [[employer]] has power over how people feel at work. Scrooge says, “The happiness he gives, is quite as great as if it cost a fortune.” The [[comparison]] with a fortune is revealing because Scrooge usually measures what things are [[worth]] in money. Here he uses money to express the value of kindness, which he has just described in [[terms]] of everyday words and looks. Dickens follows this with Scrooge’s wish to speak to Bob, showing how a [[memory]] begins to change his view of his own behaviour.

Belle presents Scrooge’s love of money as a form of [[worship]]. She tells him, “Another idol has displaced me”, before identifying it as “A golden one.” The [[verb]] “displaced” makes it sound as though money has taken a position that once belonged to Belle. By [[describing]] it as an “idol”, she suggests that he has come to trust it above [[everything]] else. Dickens lets the reader see why this matters through the loss of a relationship. The more Scrooge [[depends]] on money for security, the more isolated he becomes.

Dickens makes social problems feel [[urgent]] by giving them the bodies of children. The Ghost tells Scrooge, “This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want.” The two [[short]] sentences sound like an introduction, but the names make the children stand for problems that [[reach]] far beyond them. “Want” shows what happens when people lack basic necessities, while “Ignorance” [[suggests]] how easily others can overlook that suffering. Dickens makes both children [[vulnerable]] so the reader has to think about who has the power to help them.

When the Ghost [[answers]] Scrooge with “Are there no prisons?” and “Are there no workhouses?”, Dickens changes the force of questions we heard in Stave One. [[Earlier]], Scrooge used them to end a conversation about helping the poor. Here he has [[asked]] where two frightened children can find help, so his own words sound like a [[refusal]] to answer him. By keeping the questions familiar and changing the situation, Dickens lets the reader see how [[inadequate]] Scrooge’s solution was all along.

Dickens shows that Scrooge’s feelings about poverty are [[changing]] when he is “overcome with penitence and grief”. “Penitence” suggests regret for his own words, while “grief” shows how [[much]] he already cares about what might happen to Tiny Tim. The word “overcome” makes these feelings [[seem]] stronger than his usual habit of defending himself. By making the Ghost repeat the [[remark]] about the surplus population just before this reaction, Dickens shows the reader what happens when Scrooge hears an [[impersonal]] judgement applied to someone he knows.

When Scrooge reads “upon the stone of the [[neglected]] grave his own name, Ebenezer Scrooge”, Dickens brings his childhood and possible future together. “Neglected” first [[described]] a boy who was left alone. Now it describes a grave that nobody seems to care for. The [[placing]] of Scrooge’s name at the end of the description also makes the discovery feel [[final]]. For the reader, the repeated word raises a question about how far Scrooge has helped to continue the [[loneliness]] that began when he was a child.

Scrooge’s promise to “[[honour]] Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year” shows that his idea of Christmas has changed. The verb “honour” [[suggests]] that he now takes its values seriously, and “all the year” gives him a much longer [[task]] than celebrating one day. There is some humility in “try”, since he will have to put his promise into [[practice]]. Dickens ends the scene with Scrooge asking for that chance, so the reader can [[judge]] his words against his actions the next morning.

Dickens makes Scrooge’s joy audible through three [[similes]]. Scrooge declares, “I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a [[schoolboy]].” The repetition of “I am” gives each new comparison its own burst of [[energy]]. “Light” can remind the reader of the burden Marley still carries, while “schoolboy” recalls the [[lonely]] child Scrooge used to be. The ending gives both images a happier meaning and lets the reader [[hear]] how fully Scrooge is enjoying his second chance.

Dickens uses Bob’s fear of being told off to [[show]] how much has changed in Scrooge’s attitude to work. When Scrooge announces, “I am about to raise your salary!”, the [[exclamation]] comes just as Bob expects a punishment. Earlier, Scrooge complained about [[paying]] Bob for Christmas Day, so the raise reverses a pattern the reader has already seen. It also [[follows]] through on what Scrooge learnt from Fezziwig. He now uses his position as an [[employer]] to make life easier for someone who depends on him.

When the [[narrator]] says that “to Tiny Tim, who did not die, he was a second father”, Dickens shows that Scrooge’s [[care]] has lasted beyond Christmas Day. The words “who did not die” quietly answer the Ghost’s warning about Tim’s [[future]]. “Second father” then gives Scrooge a place in the boy’s life that goes beyond the help he gives Bob as an [[employer]]. By putting these details together, Dickens lets the reader see how Scrooge’s [[decision]] to care for others changes the future he was shown.

Dickens ends with the narrator taking up Tiny Tim’s [[blessing]], “God bless Us, Every One!” The word “Us” brings the reader into the closing wish, while “Every One” [[extends]] it to people outside the Cratchit family. That includes the man who once [[spoke]] about a “surplus population”. By ending with Tim’s words, Dickens gives the child Scrooge might once have [[dismissed]] a way to sum up what the older man has had to [[learn]]. Nobody in the blessing is treated as if they could be spared.

Dickens’s oyster simile makes Scrooge’s isolation look like a form of [[self-defence]]. The description “secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster” moves from what Scrooge [[withholds]] to the condition in which he lives. “Self-contained” can sound like a claim to [[independence]], yet the oyster’s shell suggests that such independence depends on keeping the world outside. When “solitary” reappears in the [[schoolroom]], Dickens gives this defence a history. The reader can see how a habit that once protected Scrooge might now [[perpetuate]] the loneliness it helped him endure.

Dickens makes flint an image of both Scrooge’s [[resistance]] and his capacity to change. He is “Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire”. “Hard” [[suggests]] that other people struggle to make any impression on him, while “sharp” gives him the [[power]] to wound them in return. Yet “had ever” describes the past, and the image of [[striking]] flint makes warmth something that might emerge through contact. The spirits’ visits test that possibility, as [[encounters]] Scrooge would ordinarily avoid become the means of his transformation.

Scrooge’s “Bah!” and “Humbug!” reduce a conversation about Christmas to a [[dismissal]]. The first exclamation makes his impatience audible before the second gives it the force of an [[accusation]]. To call something humbug is to suspect a pretence, so Scrooge treats Fred’s [[goodwill]] as something a sensible man should see through. Dickens places this curt verdict beside Fred’s patient [[account]] of what Christmas can do for people. The reader can see how Scrooge’s certainty about other people’s motives allows him to [[dismiss]] an invitation before he has considered what it offers.

Scrooge’s refusal to “make idle people merry” exposes the moral [[judgement]] behind his claim that he “can’t afford” to help. “Can’t” presents a choice as a financial [[necessity]], while “idle” assigns blame to the people who would benefit from his [[generosity]]. He even uses his own refusal to make merry as a reason to deny others the opportunity. Dickens revisits this narrow idea of what can be [[afforded]] through Fezziwig, whose power to give happiness lies partly in words and looks. The reader is left to [[measure]] the real cost of Scrooge’s refusal.

Scrooge answers a request for [[charity]] with “Are there no prisons?” and “And the Union workhouses?” The questions ask the gentlemen to confirm that [[institutions]] exist, a much easier question to answer than whether those institutions offer adequate help. The pairing of prisons and workhouses also [[lends]] the relief of poverty the language of punishment. When the Ghost returns to this [[exchange]] in Stave Three, Scrooge has to hear his logic applied to children. Dickens makes the reader judge a [[policy]] through the people expected to live with its consequences.

Scrooge’s claim that the poor had [[better]] die and “decrease the surplus population” borrows the language of calculation to make cruelty sound practical. “Surplus” implies a [[standard]] of how many people society needs, yet Scrooge speaks as though he has both the knowledge and the [[right]] to make that judgement. Dickens later gives his very words to the Ghost of Christmas Present, who [[applies]] them to Tiny Tim. The echo exposes what the original phrase conceals. The people treated as excess are [[particular]] human beings whose lives matter to others.

In “I wear the chain I forged in life”, Marley [[names]] himself as both the maker and the wearer of his punishment. The [[distinction]] between the present “wear” and the past “forged” connects what he suffers now to choices he once had the [[freedom]] to make. Forging takes labour, and the links suggest a burden built by repetition. Dickens gives this [[process]] a visible form so that Scrooge, who recognises his own habits in Marley’s account, can see what [[years]] of apparently ordinary business decisions might amount to.

“Mankind was my business” takes Scrooge’s praise of Marley as a [[businessman]] and makes it the basis of a rebuke. “Business” first means the work by which the [[partners]] judged their success. Marley gives it the sense of a duty, and “Mankind” places that duty far beyond the [[limits]] of the counting-house. Dickens gives this recognition to a man who can regret his [[choices]] but can no longer act on it. When Scrooge later raises Bob’s wages, the reader sees what Marley’s [[insight]] looks like while it can still do some good.

Fred’s idea that people are “fellow-passengers to the grave” brings [[mortality]] into his defence of Christmas. A fellow-passenger may be a stranger, yet the shared [[destination]] makes it harder to regard that person’s life as entirely separate from one’s own. The image challenges Scrooge’s [[confidence]] that wealth distinguishes him from the people he dismisses. When he later sees his own grave, the reader can [[hear]] Fred’s words again. Everyone faces the same end, but the affection or relief their death leaves behind [[depends]] in part on how they have travelled together.

The Ghost’s description of “A solitary child, [[neglected]] by his friends” revisits a word that the narrator first applies to the adult Scrooge. Here the [[phrases]] “neglected by” and “is left” put the emphasis on what others have done to the boy. The word “still” makes him seem [[suspended]] in a scene he has outwardly left behind. Dickens lets the reader reconsider the adult’s [[self-imposed]] isolation in light of that earlier experience. We can understand why Scrooge learned to protect himself while still holding him [[responsible]] for the way he treats others.

When Scrooge says that “The [[happiness]] he gives, is quite as great as if it cost a fortune”, he uses a comparison with money to explain the [[value]] of something he has just said is impossible to count. That tension makes the moment revealing. He still [[thinks]] in the language of business, but his memory of Fezziwig stretches what that language can express. Dickens follows the [[speech]] with Scrooge’s wish to speak to Bob, allowing the reader to see an insight into his own [[apprenticeship]] turn into a judgement about his conduct as an employer.

Belle’s claim that “Another idol has [[displaced]] me” makes Scrooge’s pursuit of money sound like an act of devotion. Calling the idol “A golden one” also invites a [[biblical]] association with the worship of the golden calf. The verb “displaced” gives the image a personal [[cost]], because Belle can name the place in Scrooge’s life that money has taken. Dickens lets her explain the [[change]] from inside the relationship. The reader can see how the security Scrooge seeks comes at the [[expense]] of someone with whom he might have shared it.

The Ghost’s declarations “This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want” [[make]] social conditions appear before Scrooge as children. The repeated “This” directs his attention to [[figures]] he might otherwise prefer to overlook. “Want” gives bodily form to the lack of basic [[necessities]], while “Ignorance” asks who has failed to see or understand that need. The Ghost singles out the boy as the [[greater]] danger, suggesting that suffering is harder to remedy when it goes unrecognised. Dickens tests the reader’s [[willingness]] to look as closely as he tests Scrooge’s.

When the Ghost [[asks]] “Are there no prisons?” and “Are there no workhouses?”, the words return to Scrooge with their speaker and audience reversed. In Stave One, such [[questions]] let him bring the appeal for charity to a close. Now Scrooge is the one asking where [[help]] can be found, and he has to accept the inadequacy of the answer he once gave. Dickens uses the [[echo]] to make the reader reconsider the first scene as well. The questions sounded [[decisive]] only while the people they concerned were kept out of sight.

By the time Scrooge is “overcome with penitence and [[grief]]”, concern for Tiny Tim has made it harder for him to defend what he said about the [[poor]]. “Grief” directs his attention towards the child’s possible death, while “penitence” sends it back towards his own words. The two nouns show that [[compassion]] involves both feeling another person’s suffering and reconsidering one’s part in it. Dickens gives the Ghost Scrooge’s exact [[argument]] about surplus population, allowing the reader to see how the same argument [[changes]] in force once its subject becomes someone Scrooge knows.

Scrooge reads “upon the stone of the [[neglected]] grave his own name, Ebenezer Scrooge”, and Dickens brings an adjective from the schoolroom into the future Scrooge [[fears]]. As a child, Scrooge was neglected by others. The grave suggests that he may die without the care he has [[spent]] much of his adult life withholding. The delayed arrival of his name makes him [[recognise]] himself in the fate he has been trying to understand. Because the vision might still be [[altered]], the echo gives the reader a pattern to watch him try to break.

Scrooge’s promise to “honour Christmas in my [[heart]], and try to keep it all the year” makes his change a commitment that must outlast the [[fear]] of the grave. “Honour” gives the promise moral weight, while “all the year” asks what becomes of Christmas [[generosity]] on ordinary days. The modest verb “try” makes the pledge feel like the beginning of a [[practice]]. Dickens lets the reader see that practice take shape when Scrooge gives money and raises Bob’s wages, [[actions]] that make his inward change visible to other people.

Dickens gives Scrooge’s joy a rhythm through the [[repeated]] “I am” in “I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an [[angel]], I am as merry as a schoolboy.” The feather suggests the lifting of a burden, which recalls the [[weight]] Marley must still carry. “Schoolboy” reaches back to Scrooge’s lonely childhood and allows him a kind of [[delight]] the earlier schoolroom scene withheld.
